screens.title: Inheritance and Polymorphism
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will learn how inheritance and polymorphism work together in Java to reduce duplication and make code flexible. You will see how a common superclass captures shared fields and methods, how subclasses extend that base with specialized behavior, and how the JVM chooses the right method at runtime using polymorphism. We will work through a running Vehicle example — Vehicle as the parent, Car and Motorcycle as child classes — and show constructor chaining with the super keyword, method overriding with @Override, and what happens when you use a superclass reference that points to a subclass object. You'll also learn common pitfalls: forgetting to call a superclass constructor when it has no default, mismatching signatures when overriding, and attempting to call subclass-only methods from a superclass reference without casting. By the end, you should be able to design small hierarchies, implement overrides safely, and reason about dynamic method dispatch. Consider a Garage holding a list of Vehicle objects that may be cars or motorcycles — polymorphism allows a single loop to call startEngine on different concrete types. What would you expect to happen when an overridden method is invoked through a superclass reference?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of the chapter you should be able to explain what inheritance is and why it models 'is-a' relationships, implement simple inheritance using the extends keyword, and describe constructor chaining using super. You will learn to spot where method overriding is appropriate, how it differs from method overloading, and why the @Override annotation is valuable for catching mistakes. Finally, you will practice polymorphism: writing code that stores subclass objects in superclass references and relying on runtime method dispatch to call the correct implementation. For example, you will be able to create a list of Vehicle references, add Car and Motorcycle instances, and iterate through the list calling startEngine and honk with confidence that the JVM will execute the right method for each object. These skills reduce duplication, make APIs extensible, and help you design cleaner object hierarchies. As you learn, watch for common pitfalls such as forgetting to call an appropriate super constructor or attempting to call subclass-only methods without casting.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Skills
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on practical skills you will use immediately. First, construct subclass objects correctly by calling the right superclass constructor with super, especially when no default exists. Second, override methods safely by matching name, return type, and parameters, and add @Override so the compiler helps you. Third, write polymorphic code that operates on a superclass type — for instance, a method accepting a Vehicle parameter can work with any subclass. Finally, perform safe downcasts using instanceof before casting to call subclass-specific methods like drive. A concrete exercise will ask you to implement a Shape hierarchy where Circle and Rectangle override calculateArea. This will exercise constructor calls, overriding signatures, and runtime polymorphism when you store shapes in a list and iterate. These abilities are essential for writing maintainable object hierarchies and avoiding runtime exceptions due to incorrect casting or missing constructors.

screens.title: What is Inheritance?
screens.narratorSegment: Inheritance is a programming mechanism where one class acquires fields and methods defined in another class. The class being inherited from is called the superclass, and the inheriting class is the subclass. In Java you express this relationship with the extends keyword: a subclass extends its superclass, which clarifies an "is-a" relationship such as Car is-a Vehicle. The practical value is reuse: attributes like brand and year, and shared methods like startEngine and stopEngine, live in one place so you avoid duplicating code in every concrete type. A common misconception is to use inheritance just to reuse code without modeling a true is-a relationship; that leads to brittle designs. Prefer inheritance when the subclass truly represents a specialized form of the superclass. Consider composition when a class merely uses another type rather than being a subtype. Concrete example: Vehicle contains brand, year, and a startEngine method; Car extends Vehicle and adds numberOfDoors and a drive method while reusing startEngine. Key takeaway: inheritance organizes behavior and state into a logical hierarchy, but should reflect real type relationships to remain maintainable. What is Inheritance? means inheritance lets a subclass reuse fields and methods from a superclass to express an "is-a" relationship and reduce duplication.. In practical terms, model shared attributes and behaviors with a superclass. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Inheritance lets a subclass reuse fields and methods from a superclass to express an "is-a" relationship and reduce duplication.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › What is Inheritance?
Concept

Inheritance captures common state and behavior in a parent so multiple child classes can reuse them.

Analogy
Think of Vehicle as a blueprint, and Car and Motorcycle as specialized versions that add features.
Concrete example
public class Vehicle {
  private String brand;
  private int year;

  public void startEngine() { /*...*/ }
}

public class Car extends Vehicle {
  private int numberOfDoors;
  public void drive() { /*...*/ }
}
Common mistake
Using inheritance for code reuse when there is no true is-a relationship causes fragile hierarchies.
Key Takeaway

Use extends to model a genuine subtype relationship and centralize shared behavior in the superclass.

How to decide
  • Check whether the subclass is truly a type of the superclass (is-a).
  • If only behavior reuse is needed, consider composition over inheritance.
  • Keep fields private and expose protected or public accessors when necessary.
Example scenario
A garage stores Vehicles. The code can hold Car and Motorcycle objects in the same collection because they share the Vehicle type.

screens.title: Using extends and super()
screens.narratorSegment: To establish inheritance in Java use the extends keyword. For example, public class Car extends Vehicle creates a subclass relationship where Car inherits Vehicle's fields and methods. A key operational detail is constructor chaining: when you instantiate a subclass, the superclass constructor must run first to initialize inherited state. You can explicitly call the desired superclass constructor using super(...) as the first statement in the subclass constructor. If you omit a call to super, Java attempts to insert a no-argument call to the superclass constructor. This becomes an error when the superclass only defines parameterized constructors, so it's important to call super with matching arguments. A concrete example from our Vehicle code: Car(String brand, int year, int numberOfDoors) calls super(brand, year) to initialize brand and year in Vehicle before setting its own fields. A common misconception is thinking super() can be placed anywhere; it must be the first statement in the constructor. Also remember super can refer to methods or fields in the superclass when needed to disambiguate a name hidden by the subclass. Takeaway: always ensure the correct superclass constructor runs to initialize inherited parts of an object.

keyIdea.title: Constructor chaining
keyIdea.text: Use super(...) at the top of a subclass constructor to call and initialize the superclass part of the object.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › extends & super()
Process: subclass construction
1. Declare subclass with extends to inherit: class Car extends Vehicle.
2. In subclass constructor, call super(...) as the first statement to run a specific superclass constructor.
3. Initialize subclass-specific fields after the super call.
4. If superclass lacks a no-arg constructor, you must call super with parameters; otherwise compilation fails.
Key Takeaway

super(...) must be the first line in a constructor when used; it ensures the superclass state is properly initialized.

Code example
public class Vehicle {
  public Vehicle(String brand, int year) {
    // initialize brand and year
  }
}

public class Car extends Vehicle {
  public Car(String brand, int year, int doors) {
    super(brand, year); // must be first
    // initialize doors
  }
}
Tip
If a superclass only has parameterized constructors, always call one from the subclass or provide a matching constructor in the superclass.

screens.title: Method Overriding — Making behavior specific
screens.narratorSegment: Method overriding is when a subclass provides a new implementation for a method defined in its superclass. The overriding method must match the name, return type, and parameter list. In Java it's best practice to annotate the method with @Override so the compiler can warn you about signature mismatches. Overriding enables polymorphism: a superclass reference can point to a subclass object and calls to the overridden method will execute the subclass version at runtime. For example, add a honk method in Vehicle that prints a generic message. In Car override honk to print a car-specific horn. If Motorcycle does not override honk, it will inherit Vehicle's implementation. A common mistake is confusing overriding with overloading — overloading provides multiple methods with different parameter lists in the same class, while overriding replaces inherited behavior. Example walkthrough: compile and run a Garage. main that creates Vehicle myCar = new Car(...); myCar. honk() will execute Car. honk at runtime. Remember to use @Override and preserve the signature exactly to avoid subtle bugs. Method Overriding — Making behavior specific means a subclass method with the same signature replaces the superclass implementation and participates in runtime dispatch.. In practical terms, override superclass methods with the same signature to specialize behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Method Overriding
Code walkthrough
// In Vehicle
public void honk() {
  System.out.println("Generic vehicle honk!");
}

// In Car
@Override
public void honk() {
  System.out.println("Car horn beeps!");
}
Explanation:
  • Use @Override to signal intent and let the compiler check the signature.
  • The JVM resolves which method to execute at runtime based on the object's actual type.
  • Overriding requires the same signature; overloading uses different parameters.
Example scenario
If myCar is declared as Vehicle but refers to a Car object, calling honk executes Car's honk because Car overrides the method. If Motorcycle doesn't override, it uses Vehicle's honk.
Common mistake
Changing return type or parameters breaks overriding; the compiler will treat it as a different method instead of an override.
Key Takeaway

Override only when the subclass truly replaces behavior; use @Override to catch mistakes early.

screens.title: Overriding vs Overloading
screens.narratorSegment: Overriding and overloading are often confused, but they serve different purposes. Overriding replaces an inherited method with a new implementation in a subclass. The method name, return type, and parameter list must match exactly. Overloading defines multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists within the same class or across an inheritance chain, providing different ways to call a method. Overriding supports polymorphism — a call to an overridden method on a superclass reference resolves at runtime to the subclass implementation. Overloading is resolved at compile time based on argument types and doesn't change runtime dispatch. A concrete contrast: if Vehicle defines honk() and Car overrides honk(), calling honk on a Vehicle reference to a Car runs Car. honk. If Vehicle had honk() and we added honk(int volume) in Car, that's overloading and does not affect calls to the no-argument honk method. Common mistake: expecting an overloaded method to substitute for an overridden one; they are separate. Use overriding when redefining behavior, and overloading to provide multiple calling options. Overriding vs Overloading means overriding replaces inherited behavior; overloading provides alternative signatures. overriding affects runtime dispatch, overloading does not.. In practical terms, distinguish replacing behavior from providing multiple signatures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Overriding vs Overloading
Overriding
  • Same name, same return type, same parameters.
  • Occurs in subclass to replace parent behavior.
  • Uses @Override to help the compiler check intent.
  • Dispatched at runtime based on actual object type.
Example
Vehicle.honk() overridden by Car.honk()
Overloading
  • Same name but different parameter lists.
  • Provides multiple ways to call a method.
  • Resolved at compile time by the compiler.
  • Does not affect runtime override behavior.
Example
honk() and honk(int volume) are different overloads.

screens.title: Polymorphism and Runtime Dispatch
screens.narratorSegment: Polymorphism lets objects of different classes related by inheritance be used interchangeably through a common superclass type. This is powerful because you can write generic code that operates on the common type while concrete implementations differ. In Java the runtime uses dynamic method dispatch to choose which overridden method to run based on the object's actual type. For example, a Garage class can hold a Vehicle reference to either a Car or a Motorcycle. When myCar. honk() runs, the JVM inspects the concrete object and calls Car. honk if overridden. This decouples calling code from concrete classes and enables extensibility: new subclasses can be added without changing the code that operates on the superclass type. A frequent error is attempting to call subclass-specific methods like drive() on a superclass reference; you must cast after verifying with instanceof. Use polymorphism when you want uniform handling for related types, and keep subclass-specific behavior accessible through safe casts or visitor-style patterns. In practice, collections like List make polymorphism tangible and concise. Polymorphism and Runtime Dispatch means treat different subclass objects as their common superclass type and rely on the jvm to resolve overridden methods at runtime.. In practical terms, use a common type to treat multiple concrete types uniformly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Polymorphism
Architecture: common interfaces
Design your classes so a single type captures shared behavior. Use lists, method parameters, and APIs typed to the superclass for flexibility.
public static void main(String[] args) {
  Vehicle myCar = new Car("Toyota", 2022, 4);
  Vehicle myMotorcycle = new Motorcycle("Harley", 2020, false);

  myCar.honk();        // Car.honk() if overridden
  myMotorcycle.honk(); // Vehicle.honk() if not overridden
}
Note
Storing different concrete types in an array or list typed to the superclass enables uniform processing of related objects.
Example: List of Vehicles
List vehicles = new ArrayList<>();
vehicles.add(new Car("Toyota", 2022, 4));
vehicles.add(new Motorcycle("Harley", 2020, false));
for (Vehicle v : vehicles) {
  v.startEngine();
  v.honk();
}
Misconception
Polymorphism does not allow calling subclass-only methods directly on a superclass reference without casting.

screens.title: Garage Example and Safe Casting
screens.narratorSegment: When you store subclass objects in a superclass reference you lose direct access to subclass-only methods, because the compiler only allows calls defined on the reference type. To access specific behavior like drive() on a Car, you must downcast the reference to the concrete subclass. Before casting, check the object with instanceof to avoid a ClassCastException. For example, if you have Vehicle myCar = new Car(...); myCar. drive() is a compile error because Vehicle does not define drive. Instead, use if (myCar instanceof Car) { Car specific = (Car) myCar; specific. drive(); } This pattern is common and safe when combined with an instanceof guard. Another approach is to design shared methods in the superclass or define an interface for shared behavior to avoid downcasts. The Garage example shows a list of Vehicle objects where we call startEngine and honk polymorphically, then perform an instanceof check to call drive only on cars. Remember: overuse of casting can signal a design that should be refactored toward shared methods or interfaces. Garage Example and Safe Casting means use instanceof to verify the actual type before casting a superclass reference to a subclass to call subclass-specific methods.. In practical terms, how instanceof and casting let you access subclass-specific methods. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: @Override and Compiler Safety
screens.narratorSegment: The @Override annotation is not required but strongly recommended when you intend to override a superclass method. It tells the compiler you expect this method to override a method in a parent class. If the method signature does not match, the compiler will report an error, preventing a silent mistake where you intended to override but instead declared a new method. For example, if you write @Override public void honk(int volume) but the superclass defines honk() with no parameters, the compiler will alert you to the mismatch. This simple practice catches many common errors and saves debugging time. Another related detail is access level: you cannot reduce visibility when overriding; a public method in the superclass must remain public in the subclass. Also check return types: for object types you may use covariant returns where the overridden method returns a subtype. Use @Override consistently when you override methods to make your intent explicit and keep your code robust. @Override and Compiler Safety means annotate overrides with @override so the compiler verifies your signature and prevents accidental overloading.. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Shape Exercise
Starter code: Shape
public class Shape {
  private String color;

  public Shape(String color) {
    this.color = color;
  }

  public String getColor() { return this.color; }

  // This method will be overridden by subclasses
  public double calculateArea() {
    System.out.println("Calculating area for a generic shape (should be overridden).");
    return 0.0;
  }
}
Starter code: ShapeCalculator
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class ShapeCalculator {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    Circle myCircle = new Circle("Red", 5.0);
    Rectangle myRectangle = new Rectangle("Blue", 4.0, 6.0);

    List shapes = new ArrayList<>();
    shapes.add(myCircle);
    shapes.add(myRectangle);

    for (Shape shape : shapes) {
      System.out.println("Shape Color: " + shape.getColor());
      System.out.println("Shape Area: " + shape.calculateArea());
      System.out.println("---");
    }
  }
}
Key Takeaway

This exercise solidifies how overriding and polymorphism let a single algorithm handle multiple concrete implementations cleanly.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Several recurring mistakes appear when learning inheritance and polymorphism. First, forgetting to call super(...) in a subclass constructor when the superclass does not have a no-argument constructor will cause a compile-time error. Always inspect superclass constructors and call an appropriate one from your subclass. Second, method overriding requires an identical signature; changing parameters or return types unintentionally creates a new method instead of overriding. Using @Override helps detect this early. Third, attempting to call subclass-specific methods from a superclass reference results in compile-time errors; you must cast after an instanceof check to be safe. Fourth, confusing overriding with overloading leads to unexpected behavior since overloading does not affect runtime dispatch. Fifth, reducing visibility in an override is illegal — a public method must remain public. To avoid these, write clear constructors, add @Override annotations, design proper interfaces for shared behavior, and minimize casts by pushing shared contracts into the superclass or interfaces. These simple practices make hierarchies robust and easier to maintain. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the most important concepts. Inheritance lets a subclass acquire the fields and methods of a superclass and models an is-a relationship; use extends when that relationship is appropriate. The super keyword is used to call superclass constructors and to refer to superclass members when needed, and super(...) must be the first line in a constructor call. Method overriding lets a subclass provide a specialized implementation for an inherited method; annotate it with @Override so the compiler can detect mismatches. Overloading is different: it provides multiple parameter lists and is resolved at compile time. Polymorphism allows a single superclass reference to refer to subclass objects; the JVM dispatches overridden methods according to the object's actual type at runtime. Use instanceof and casting to access subclass-specific methods safely, or design shared methods or interfaces to avoid casts. These principles help you write reusable, extensible, and maintainable object-oriented code.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will learn how inheritance and polymorphism work together in Java to reduce duplication and make code flexible. You will see how a common superclass captures shared fields and methods, how subclasses extend that base with specialized behavior, and how the JVM chooses the right method at runtime using polymorphism. We will work through a running Vehicle example — Vehicle as the parent, Car and Motorcycle as child classes — and show constructor chaining with the super keyword, method overriding with @Override, and what happens when you use a superclass reference that points to a subclass object. You'll also learn common pitfalls: forgetting to call a superclass constructor when it has no default, mismatching signatures when overriding, and attempting to call subclass-only methods from a superclass reference without casting. By the end, you should be able to design small hierarchies, implement overrides safely, and reason about dynamic method dispatch. Consider a Garage holding a list of Vehicle objects that may be cars or motorcycles — polymorphism allows a single loop to call startEngine on different concrete types. What would you expect to happen when an overridden method is invoked through a superclass reference?

By the end of the chapter you should be able to explain what inheritance is and why it models 'is-a' relationships, implement simple inheritance using the extends keyword, and describe constructor chaining using super. You will learn to spot where method overriding is appropriate, how it differs from method overloading, and why the @Override annotation is valuable for catching mistakes. Finally, you will practice polymorphism: writing code that stores subclass objects in superclass references and relying on runtime method dispatch to call the correct implementation. For example, you will be able to create a list of Vehicle references, add Car and Motorcycle instances, and iterate through the list calling startEngine and honk with confidence that the JVM will execute the right method for each object. These skills reduce duplication, make APIs extensible, and help you design cleaner object hierarchies. As you learn, watch for common pitfalls such as forgetting to call an appropriate super constructor or attempting to call subclass-only methods without casting.

These objectives focus on practical skills you will use immediately. First, construct subclass objects correctly by calling the right superclass constructor with super, especially when no default exists. Second, override methods safely by matching name, return type, and parameters, and add @Override so the compiler helps you. Third, write polymorphic code that operates on a superclass type — for instance, a method accepting a Vehicle parameter can work with any subclass. Finally, perform safe downcasts using instanceof before casting to call subclass-specific methods like drive. A concrete exercise will ask you to implement a Shape hierarchy where Circle and Rectangle override calculateArea. This will exercise constructor calls, overriding signatures, and runtime polymorphism when you store shapes in a list and iterate. These abilities are essential for writing maintainable object hierarchies and avoiding runtime exceptions due to incorrect casting or missing constructors.

Inheritance is a programming mechanism where one class acquires fields and methods defined in another class. The class being inherited from is called the superclass, and the inheriting class is the subclass. In Java you express this relationship with the extends keyword: a subclass extends its superclass, which clarifies an "is-a" relationship such as Car is-a Vehicle. The practical value is reuse: attributes like brand and year, and shared methods like startEngine and stopEngine, live in one place so you avoid duplicating code in every concrete type. A common misconception is to use inheritance just to reuse code without modeling a true is-a relationship; that leads to brittle designs. Prefer inheritance when the subclass truly represents a specialized form of the superclass. Consider composition when a class merely uses another type rather than being a subtype. Concrete example: Vehicle contains brand, year, and a startEngine method; Car extends Vehicle and adds numberOfDoors and a drive method while reusing startEngine. Key takeaway: inheritance organizes behavior and state into a logical hierarchy, but should reflect real type relationships to remain maintainable. What is Inheritance? means inheritance lets a subclass reuse fields and methods from a superclass to express an "is-a" relationship and reduce duplication.. In practical terms, model shared attributes and behaviors with a superclass. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

To establish inheritance in Java use the extends keyword. For example, public class Car extends Vehicle creates a subclass relationship where Car inherits Vehicle's fields and methods. A key operational detail is constructor chaining: when you instantiate a subclass, the superclass constructor must run first to initialize inherited state. You can explicitly call the desired superclass constructor using super(...) as the first statement in the subclass constructor. If you omit a call to super, Java attempts to insert a no-argument call to the superclass constructor. This becomes an error when the superclass only defines parameterized constructors, so it's important to call super with matching arguments. A concrete example from our Vehicle code: Car(String brand, int year, int numberOfDoors) calls super(brand, year) to initialize brand and year in Vehicle before setting its own fields. A common misconception is thinking super() can be placed anywhere; it must be the first statement in the constructor. Also remember super can refer to methods or fields in the superclass when needed to disambiguate a name hidden by the subclass. Takeaway: always ensure the correct superclass constructor runs to initialize inherited parts of an object.

Method overriding is when a subclass provides a new implementation for a method defined in its superclass. The overriding method must match the name, return type, and parameter list. In Java it's best practice to annotate the method with @Override so the compiler can warn you about signature mismatches. Overriding enables polymorphism: a superclass reference can point to a subclass object and calls to the overridden method will execute the subclass version at runtime. For example, add a honk method in Vehicle that prints a generic message. In Car override honk to print a car-specific horn. If Motorcycle does not override honk, it will inherit Vehicle's implementation. A common mistake is confusing overriding with overloading — overloading provides multiple methods with different parameter lists in the same class, while overriding replaces inherited behavior. Example walkthrough: compile and run a Garage. main that creates Vehicle myCar = new Car(...); myCar. honk() will execute Car. honk at runtime. Remember to use @Override and preserve the signature exactly to avoid subtle bugs. Method Overriding — Making behavior specific means a subclass method with the same signature replaces the superclass implementation and participates in runtime dispatch.. In practical terms, override superclass methods with the same signature to specialize behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Overriding and overloading are often confused, but they serve different purposes. Overriding replaces an inherited method with a new implementation in a subclass. The method name, return type, and parameter list must match exactly. Overloading defines multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists within the same class or across an inheritance chain, providing different ways to call a method. Overriding supports polymorphism — a call to an overridden method on a superclass reference resolves at runtime to the subclass implementation. Overloading is resolved at compile time based on argument types and doesn't change runtime dispatch. A concrete contrast: if Vehicle defines honk() and Car overrides honk(), calling honk on a Vehicle reference to a Car runs Car. honk. If Vehicle had honk() and we added honk(int volume) in Car, that's overloading and does not affect calls to the no-argument honk method. Common mistake: expecting an overloaded method to substitute for an overridden one; they are separate. Use overriding when redefining behavior, and overloading to provide multiple calling options. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Polymorphism lets objects of different classes related by inheritance be used interchangeably through a common superclass type. This is powerful because you can write generic code that operates on the common type while concrete implementations differ. In Java the runtime uses dynamic method dispatch to choose which overridden method to run based on the object's actual type. For example, a Garage class can hold a Vehicle reference to either a Car or a Motorcycle. When myCar. honk() runs, the JVM inspects the concrete object and calls Car. honk if overridden. Let's summarize the most important concepts. Inheritance lets a subclass acquire the fields and methods of a superclass and models an is-a relationship; use extends when that relationship is appropriate. The super keyword is used to call superclass constructors and to refer to superclass members when needed, and super(...) must be the first line in a constructor call. Method overriding lets a subclass provide a specialized implementation for an inherited method; annotate it with @Override so the compiler can detect mismatches. Overloading is different: it provides multiple parameter lists and is resolved at compile time. Polymorphism allows a single superclass reference to refer to subclass objects; the JVM dispatches overridden methods according to the object's actual type at runtime. Use instanceof and casting to access subclass-specific methods safely, or design shared methods or interfaces to avoid casts. These principles help you write reusable, extensible, and maintainable object-oriented code.

A concise reference helps while coding. Remember: extends creates an is-a relation. Use super(...) as the first line in a subclass constructor to invoke a specific superclass constructor. Annotate overridden methods with @Override so the compiler validates your intent. Use instanceof before downcasting and prefer shared methods or interfaces to avoid casts when possible. Overloading is compile-time polymorphism with different parameter lists; overriding is runtime polymorphism where the JVM chooses the subclass method. Finally, when in doubt about a design that needs many casts, consider refactoring to move common behavior into the superclass or define an interface that describes the shared contract.
